lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Tiago (Mock Rodízio) | Lesson 3 -- Two Suppliers, One Slot

reading.rtitle: One production slot, two ways to fill it
paras: You have one free production slot in October and two quotes on your desk. Both suppliers can make the bracket. Only one of them can have the slot, and purchasing wants your recommendation by Friday.

Delta Metal has supplied you for six years. Their unit price is 4.20 dollars, with a minimum order of 5,000 pieces and a lead time of four weeks. They hold the ISO certification your American customer asks for, and in six years they have missed two dates, both by less than a week. Their quote ends with a line you have read many times: any delay above five days carries a penalty clause of 2% of the order value.

Krammer is new. Their unit price is 3.65 dollars, thirteen percent below Delta, with a minimum order of 12,000 pieces and a lead time of six weeks. Their capacity is larger and they say they can absorb a second order later in the year. Their quote says nothing about certification, and there is no penalty clause in it — in either direction.
You called two companies who use Krammer. The first said they are good and cheap and answer the phone. The second said the first six months were difficult, and then it settled.

The saving, if you go with Krammer, is about seven thousand dollars on this order. Your customer's audit is in March, and you do not yet know whether they will ask for the certificate of every supplier in the chain, or only of yours.

gist.prompt: What is the real decision here?
choices: Which supplier is cheaper for this order.
Whether the saving is worth a supplier with no track record and no certification on paper.
Whether to produce in October or move the slot.

language.title: Analyse and answer
items: Line 5 says should save around, not will save. What would change for your boss if you said will?
Line 1 puts the good news first and the problem after but. What happens if you swap them?
Lines 3 and 6 both talk about risk. What is the difference between what worries you and what you cannot cover?
Which of the six would you never say to a customer, only to your own boss?

language.title: Reveal answer key
list: Will save promises a number you do not control. Should save around commits to the estimate without owning the outcome — and it is the difference between being trusted twice and being trusted once.
Swapping them changes the recommendation: what comes after but is what the listener remembers.
What worries me is a feeling you can act on. What I cannot cover is a fact about the limits of your job — it moves the decision to whoever can cover it.
Line 11 ("never had a problem is not the same as never having a risk") — internally it is honest; to a customer it sounds like doubt about your own supplier.
language.note: Do not drill these lines and do not correct his form here. This stage is exposure; the form is refined after the task.

items: The situation
Purchasing wants a recommendation by Friday: Delta or Krammer for the October slot. Your teacher is the plant manager, who has worked with Delta for six years and does not want to change.
Plan first — 2 minutes, out loud
Choose ONE supplier and name the three points you will use. "It is cheaper" is not a point on its own: cheaper than what, and at what cost? Say the three out loud before you start.
Then recommend — the tangible outcome
By the end, you and the plant manager must have said out loud: (1) which supplier gets the slot, (2) the one condition that would change your mind, and (3) who carries the risk if it goes wrong.
Report — to your customer, alone
Your teacher stops being the plant manager. In 90 seconds, uninterrupted, report the decision the way you would tell Michael: what you chose, what it costs him, and the risk that is still open.

task1.title: What the report has to contain
items: The recommendation in one sentence, at the start — not at the end.
The trade-off, named. If you gained something, say what you gave up for it.
The risk you did NOT close, said plainly and without hedging it away.
What you need from him: a decision, a date, or a number.

task1.label: Useful language
items: The main trade-off is...
What worries me is...
If we go with Krammer, we...
It should save around...
The risk I can't cover is...
That would only matter if...
I can live with the price if we fix the lead time.
I'd rather pay more and sleep.
The situation changes
Michael has just moved the delivery two weeks earlier. Krammer's six-week lead time no longer fits the October slot; Delta's four weeks fits, but only if the order goes in on Monday.
The three options

(1) Delta, order Monday, no time to negotiate the price. (2) Krammer anyway, and tell Michael the date moves. (3) Split the order: Delta now for what he needs first, Krammer later for the rest — two setups, two invoices, more work for you.

task2.title: Decide out loud
items: Which option, and what is the first sentence you say to Michael?
If this changes what you recommended ten minutes ago, say so out loud — and say what made you change.
Option 3 costs you personally, in your own time. Does that belong in the recommendation? Why, or why not?
What would have to be true for you to go back to your first answer?

task2.text: Your teacher will take the opposite view and give you one hard objection. Hold your position in English — or change it, and say what changed it.

wrapup.title: Before you go
items: Say your recommendation again, in one sentence, the way you would open the call.
Name the trade-off in six words or fewer.
Which decision at your work this month deserves the same 90-second report?
